stories.topic: La Noche Triste — The Night the Aztecs Drove Cortés Out (1520)
stories.footnote: The famous "Tree of the Night of Sorrows" where Cortés supposedly sat and wept became a colonial landmark — but the larger truth is that this was one of the rare moments in the conquest when Indigenous forces decisively shattered the myth of Spanish invincibility.

stories.topic: The Night Edo Burned — The Great Fire of Meireki (1657)
stories.footnote: The fire killed so many people so quickly that the Tokugawa shogunate responded not just with rebuilding, but with urban redesign — wider streets, firebreaks, and new zoning rules that helped shape Edo into the city that would eventually become Tokyo.

stories.topic: The Antikythera Mechanism — The Machine Out of Time (c. 70–60 BC)
stories.footnote: The mechanism's gear train models the Moon's irregular orbit with remarkable fidelity — its teeth are cut to account for the fact that the Moon moves faster when it is closer to Earth; no one expected the Greeks to have understood this, and for a long time, no one believed they had.

stories.topic: The Siege of Vienna — The Last Charge of the Winged Hussars (1683)
stories.region: Central Europe / Habsburg Empire / Ottoman Empire
stories.footnote: The coffee houses of Vienna trace their origin to sacks of coffee beans left behind in the Ottoman camp — one of the strangest and most pleasant spoils of war in European history

stories.topic: The Wayfinders — Polynesian Navigation Across the Pacific
stories.footnote: The Polynesian word for 'lost' — in the navigational sense — does not exist in most Pacific Island languages; the concept was, quite literally, unthinkable

stories.topic: The Tulip That Ate Holland — Dutch Tulip Mania
stories.footnote: The word 'bourse' — meaning stock exchange — comes from the Bruges home of the Van der Beurze family, where medieval merchants gathered to trade; the Dutch tulip traders who crashed the world's first speculative bubble were, in a sense, just the grandchildren of that invention

stories.topic: The Fall of Singapore — The Night the Empire Died
stories.footnote: Yamashita's troops were so low on supplies that his chief of staff later admitted the surrender came 'just in time' — had Percival held out another week, the Japanese might have been forced to withdraw

stories.topic: Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Valley — The City With No King
stories.footnote: The Indus Valley civilisation used standardised weights in multiples of 0.87 grams — a system so precise that a merchant in Harappa and a merchant in Lothal, 800 miles apart, could trade without dispute

stories.topic: Great Zimbabwe — The Stone City That Shouldn't Exist
stories.footnote: Great Zimbabwe's walls contain no mortar whatsoever — every stone holds its place through nothing but gravity and the precision of its cut

stories.topic: The Inca Quipu — An Empire Run on Knotted String
stories.footnote: The Inca empire had no markets — the state distributed everything, making it history's largest planned economy until the twentieth century

stories.topic: The Ink That Darkened the Tigris — The Fall of Baghdad (1258)
stories.footnote: The Arabic word 'algebra' — from al-jabr — survived the sack of Baghdad inside a treatise that had already been translated into Latin in Spain two centuries before Hulagu arrived; the Mongols destroyed the city, but the mathematics had already escaped.

stories.topic: The King Who Burned the Sea — Rajendra Chola and the Raid on Srivijaya (1025)
stories.region: South India / Southeast Asia / Indian Ocean
stories.footnote: Rajendra Chola commemorated his overseas triumph not with a sea fort or a captured throne, but by building a new capital called Gangaikonda Cholapuram — 'the city of the Chola who took the Ganges' — linking conquest by river and conquest by sea into one imperial boast.
